name: Pin Art
basis: why: pins slide back to an object's height and raked light turns height into shade; how: pin heights from brightness, shaded round heads
note: Interactive and animated; the desk toy and Alexeieff's pinscreen share the principle.

lumenary.blurb: The desk toy of a thousand loose metal pins. Each pin slides out as far as the picture is bright, so the picture stands up as a relief of shining heads. Press into it with the cursor and the pins sink, then spring back. On video the pins follow every frame.

facts.from: The pinscreen of animators, and the desk toy
facts.era: Pinscreen animation from 1933, the desk toy from 1985
facts.bestOn: Pictures with strong light and dark shapes, and faces in side light

why: A bed of loose pins is a screen made of depth. Press an object into it and every pin slides back by exactly as much as the object is high, so the surface becomes a copy of its shape. Lit from one side, the round heads turn that copy into light and shadow: the taller the pin, the more light it catches. Here the picture decides how high each pin stands, so brightness becomes height, and height becomes brightness again.
how: Divide the picture into a grid of pins and give each the average brightness of its square, with the contrast lifted.
Let every pin chase that brightness like a spring: it overshoots a little and settles.
Add a slow ripple, and push down the pins near the cursor so that a hand seems to press into the bed.
Draw each head as a small shaded sphere lit from the upper left, with a bright highlight.
Make taller pins larger, brighter and glossier, and leave the gaps between them dark.
history: The pinscreen was invented by the animators Alexandre Alexeieff and Claire Parker, who built the first one in Paris around 1931 and used it for the short film A Night on Bald Mountain (1933). Hundreds of thousands of pins stood in a board, and light raked across them from the side drew the picture in shadow. The toy version, with loose pins that take the shape of a hand pressed into it, was patented by Ward Fleming in 1985 and has sat on desks ever since.
uses: Desk toys and gift shop props
terms: A sculpture whose shapes stand out from a flat background instead of standing free.
The small bright spot where a shiny surface mirrors the light source.
A force that pulls something back towards a rest position in proportion to how far it has moved.
paragraphs: Each pin is a damped spring chasing a target height. The target comes from the brightness l of the picture over the pin, with the contrast lifted: t = clamp(1.3 (l - 0.5) + 0.5)^0.8, or 1 minus that if the dark parts should stand out, plus a travelling ripple 0.08 w sin(2 pi (1.3 x/n_x + 0.9 y/n_y) - 1.5 tau), with w the ripple slider and tau the time. The height h obeys h'' = k (t - h) - c h', stepped in pieces of at most 16 ms. The springiness slider sets k between 60 and 14 and the damping c from just over critical to about a third of it, which is the difference between a pin that creeps into place and one that rebounds.

The cursor is a Gaussian of width 0.075 of the picture. Where it is, a pin is pushed down at once to a cap of 1 - g, where g is the Gaussian times a hold factor that eases to 1 while the cursor is inside; its velocity is cut so that it does not bounce upward, and the spring takes it back as the cursor moves on. Each pin is then drawn in its cell as a sphere of radius rho = 0.6 + 0.33 H, where H is its height times the relief slider. The normal at offset (u, v) is (u, v, sqrt(rho^2 - u^2 - v^2)) / rho; the diffuse term is its dot product with the light direction (-0.42, -0.52, 0.74), normalised, and the highlight is (2 n_z (n . L) - L_z)^36, stronger for tall pins. The head is brightened by (0.3 + 0.9 diffuse)(0.3 + 1.05 H), and the gap between pins is near black with a thin rim of light on the shaft of tall ones.

equations.note: A pin chases its target t; s is the springiness slider (0 to 1).
A head’s radius grows with its height H, and its normal follows the sphere.

equations.tex: B=(0.3+0.9\,\mathbf n\!\cdot\!\mathbf L)(0.3+1.05\,H),\qquad S=(2n_z\,\mathbf n\!\cdot\!\mathbf L-L_z)^{36}

dials.label: Pins stand out where the picture is

presets.text: Brass pins and a tall relief make a convincing metal wall panel.
Fine pins in the picture’s own colours turn it into a glittering bead screen.
Stand the dark parts forward to see a portrait as if cast in a mould.
